body:
For those that come after me, you can't set a value higher than 1.0 through the editor, but the underlying node setters don't clamp the value, so you can set a value higher than 1.0 in your node's ready function to get much higher values.

It's not an ideal workaround, but it does work.

Godot and Jolt seem to use different definitions of damping, godot:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/a8ece29adcf639305da073554be5cb1a7916b42b/modules/godot_physics_3d/godot_soft_body_3d.cpp#L1087-L1095

So:

```
vc = (1.0 - damping_coefficient) / delta_time
```

and

```
node.v = (node.x - node.q) * vc
```

or in English:

```
new_velocity = (particle_position - old_particle_position) / delta_time * (1 - damping_coefficient)
```

or

```
new_velocity = old_velocity * (1 - damping_coefficient)
```

This means that with a damping coefficient of 1, the particle stops in 1 update, regardless of how large the delta time step is. For damping coefficients > 1, the velocity flips. This is a very unconventional way of defining damping.

Usually you define damping to be proportional to the current velocity, e.g.:

```
dv/dt = -damping_coefficient * v
```

Where dv/dt is the time derivative of velocity, integrating this you get:

```
new_velocity = old_velocity * e^(-damping_coefficient * delta_time)
```

Where e = 2.718... For small delta_time this is approximately equal to:

```
new_velocity = old_velocity * (1 - damping_coefficient * delta_time)
```

This is exactly the formula that Jolt is using:

https://github.com/jrouwe/JoltPhysics/blob/454f56b2c62e1121fce54b7ced5609926175339d/Jolt/Physics/SoftBody/SoftBodyMotionProperties.cpp#L315-L327

(well, almost, it clamps the factor so that it cannot become negative and flip the velocity)

For normal rigid bodies, godot does use the same dampening formula as Jolt as can be seen here:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/a8ece29adcf639305da073554be5cb1a7916b42b/modules/godot_physics_3d/godot_body_3d.cpp#L636-L640

So I believe that the code in godot_soft_body_3d contains a bug and that this:

```
const real_t vc = (1.0 - damping_coefficient) * inv_delta; 
```

should actually have been:

```
const real_t vc = max(inv_delta - damping_coefficient, 0.0);
```

Obviously that changes the behavior of godot physics, so it's a question if we want to fix this or not. In any case, it also gives us a formula to convert godot damping values to Jolt damping values:

```
jolt_damping = godot_damping / delta_time
```

So if you run your simulation at 60Hz you need to make your damping values 60 times bigger to achieve the same effect with Jolt as in godot.

*Note: I speak as a layman here with very surface-level understanding of the math here and implementation used by Godot for different bodies. I just recall this being discussed in the past so I'm trying to bring some extra context.*

Godot's damping coefficient are indeed unconventional, but I wonder if that isn't intentional, for better or worse. We can evaluate changing them but that will break compatibility for existing projects.

The current coefficient seems to be a ratio and limited to the `[0; 1]` range, i.e. going from no damping to max damping:
```
ADD_PROPERTY(PropertyInfo(Variant::FLOAT, "damping_coefficient", PROPERTY_HINT_RANGE, "0,1,0.01"), "set_damping_coefficient", "get_damping_coefficient");
```

So what OP points out is that with Jolt it's not possible to achieve what could be done with Godot, as the max value is 1.0. The clamping would need to be removed to allow going above 1.0.

I remember similar issues back in Godot 3.x with Bullet discussed in depth in #37314.

CC @godotengine/physics

Looking at 37314 the diff affects this area:

https://github.com/bulletphysics/bullet3/blob/d1a4256b3a019117f2bb6cb8c63d6367aaf512e2/src/BulletDynamics/Dynamics/btRigidBody.cpp#L137-L160

Basically, after the change `BT_USE_OLD_DAMPING_METHOD` is set, which means it switches from using:

```
new_velocity = old_velocity * e^(-damping_coefficient * delta_time)
```

to the approximation:

```
new_velocity = old_velocity * (1 - damping_coefficient * delta_time)
```

Apparently Bullet made the switch from approximation to accurate version and that caused undesired differences in godot that were rolled back with this change. In any case, this is for rigid bodies, not for soft bodies.

As far as I can see, the very first version of soft body 3d already had the calculation that it currently has and it seems to be taken from equivalent code in Bullet:

https://github.com/bulletphysics/bullet3/blob/d1a4256b3a019117f2bb6cb8c63d6367aaf512e2/src/BulletSoftBody/btSoftBody.cpp#L2265-L2271

which contains the same "bug" (I say bug because I don't think damping should be frame rate dependent).
